change_requests.title: Progressive runtime quote loop is leaving some visible tape symbols without populated values
evidence: During the fresh 1-7 VM rerun on 2026-05-21, the desktop scene showed moving graph cards and some live tape values, but multiple user-visible tape positions still rendered symbol-only placeholders without quote values.
The user specifically observed that the 2nd and 4th tapes were still not populating with values in the visible VM run.

In build/vm/artifacts/ssh-runs/ux-deep-ssh-20260521-121118, progressive quote hydration clearly resumed for some symbols, but not all symbols visible in the active tape layout received runtime quote fills during the sampled run window.

Combined trace evidence shows QuoteRefreshPlan repeatedly marking symbols such as QUAL, VLUE, SIZE, USMV, INTF, EMGF, SYLD, XLF, XLY, XLE, SMH, and CIBR as due, while requested_symbols and provider-return traces disproportionately favored neighboring symbols and left some visible tape symbols unfilled.
notes: This bug remains after removing QuoteCacheService and after removing SupportedQuoteSources / SupportedHistorySources multi-source gating, so the remaining issue is not the old app-side quote cache race and not the old source-profile filtering logic.
The problem currently looks like a runtime scheduling or symbol-selection defect between the visible tape model, the due-symbol planning logic, and the one-by-one progressive quote request loop.

Audit the full path from tape composition through quote scheduling and scene application, including StartupCoordinator, tape view-model generation, due-symbol selection, and the code that chooses the next symbol(s) for YFinance.NET requests.

Instrument the runtime more deeply if needed so each tape lane reports: visible symbols, symbols considered due, symbols actually requested, symbols returned, and symbols finally applied to the rendered lane.

change_requests.title: Simplify background configuration and default-background download/cache flow
evidence: User requested a CR to remove excess background configuration surface area, harden custom-folder selection, simplify the default downloaded-background flow, and investigate GPU usage after observed blank-background and transition-jitter symptoms.
notes: Settings.CustomBackgroundImageFolder must be displayed with a Choose... button next to it. The Choose... button is disabled unless Settings.UseCustomBackgroundImageFolder is checked.

The custom-background-folder text box must be read-only/non-editable by direct typing. Folder changes must come through a folder-selection dialog launched by Choose..., and the selected folder path should populate the text box.
Settings.BackgroundChangeSeconds slider minimum must become 120 seconds.
Settings.BackgroundIncludeSubfolders must default to true. It is acceptable for this setting to remain absent from the configuration screen.
Remove the Managed cache folder field from the configuration screen because it is internal storage and should not be user-visible.

Audit and enforce that the local-vs-downloaded background distinction applies only when Settings.UseCustomBackgroundImageFolder is false. When a custom folder is enabled, the selector should use only the user's configured folder, honoring BackgroundIncludeSubfolders.
Rewrite the default non-custom background logic to stay simple: ship with only three bundled backgrounds and maintain one manifest of downloadable background URLs for all additional rotating images.

Downloaded backgrounds should visually match the financial-dashboard mood: cinematic night or blue-hour global financial districts, dense illuminated skylines, reflective water or glass where possible, modern exchange buildings where visually strong, and cool blue/teal high-contrast imagery similar to the user's Chicago skyline reference. Avoid daylight tourist-postcard imagery unless it is architecturally exceptional and still reads as finance/mission-control.
Default warm-up behavior must delete any stale partial .TMP image downloads before starting new download work.

Default warm-up behavior must start a low-priority background task/thread that downloads missing manifest images to .TMP files first, then atomically renames each file to its final extension only after the complete download succeeds.
Do not redownload manifest images that already exist as complete final files from prior runs.

After one or more downloads complete, notify or invalidate the background selector so it rescans the local downloaded-image directory. Newly downloaded images do not need to be activated immediately; they can enter normal rotation later.
Before testing this CR, clear the downloaded background image directory so the harness proves first-run download behavior, .TMP cleanup, final-file rename behavior, and selector rescan behavior.

Avoid direct rotation to remote HTTP/HTTPS image URLs. The active rotation pool should contain local bundled images and completely downloaded local cache files only, preventing blank/gray frames while WPF waits for remote image pixels.
Remove any advanced layering or over-complicated background-selection logic that is not required for the current baseline behavior.

Investigate whether background rendering and transitions are using available WPF/GPU acceleration effectively. If safe, prefer GPU-friendly image caching, decoding, opacity animation, and transform choices that reduce scene jitter.

If an active background image license requires visible attribution, append the attribution to the bottom-left author/copyright text in the same unobtrusive footer style rather than adding a new overlay region.

change_requests.title: Extract a clean service-ready data engine boundary between retrieval/orchestration and UI rendering
evidence: User requested a major refactor to cleanly separate data retrieval from UI rendering so the architecture can later support a Windows service and more controlled provider parallelism.
notes: Superseded in Beta 5.6 by NB-031, which replaces the earlier in-process DataEngine / optional Windows service direction with a cleaner client-server architecture centered on an external YFinance.NET server process and a thinner UI client.

Manual code-review validation summary: the core diagnosis remains correct, but the ticket must explicitly account for three seams that are easy to underestimate. First, StartupCoordinator is not just long; it directly constructs concrete infrastructure such as multiple provider implementations, ProviderHealthService, FinanceNewsService, VisualizerSettingsService, SymbolProfileStore, and ExchangePhotoCacheService. At the time of that review it also still constructed QuoteCacheService, but that app-level quote cache has since been removed. Second, settings, secrets, traces, and caches are still user-profile rooted through PathHelper and ProviderSecretStoreService, which means a future service-ready engine needs explicit settings/secrets abstractions rather than assuming those concerns can stay ambient. Third, several orchestration types still live under the PortfolioSaver.Presentation.Services namespace even though the product is desktop-first, so namespace and composition cleanup should be treated as part of the refactor rather than deferred as mere polish.

Current diagnosis: the repository already has a meaningful provider layer under src/PortfolioSaver.Data and domain models under src/PortfolioSaver.Core, but the main runtime orchestration still lives in src/PortfolioSaver.Presentation/Services/StartupCoordinator.cs. StartupCoordinator is approximately 1800 lines and currently owns quote scheduling, provider fallback ordering, startup warmup policy, graph warmup, news refresh orchestration, cache usage, freshness logic, tracing, and scene-shaping decisions. VisualizerSceneControl is over 2100 lines and still depends on some of that orchestration behavior directly. FinanceNewsService and VisualizerSettingsService also sit in the same runtime namespace, reinforcing that the retrieval/runtime layer is not yet cleanly separated from the product surface.

The goal of this ticket is not merely to prepare for a future Windows service. The deeper goal is to establish a stable architectural seam that improves concurrency, testability, startup behavior, scheduling clarity, and future maintainability while keeping the existing desktop product working throughout the migration.

Target architecture: keep PortfolioSaver.Core for immutable models, enums, validation rules, and provider policy definitions; keep PortfolioSaver.Data for raw provider clients, caches, symbol metadata, and persistence helpers; introduce a new middle layer such as PortfolioSaver.DataEngine for quote scheduling, provider execution planning, budget/rate-limit enforcement, snapshot aggregation, startup/warmup policy, historical warmup coordination, and news scheduling; leave PortfolioSaver.Presentation focused on view-model shaping, animation, scene-state rendering, and UX display policy. Introduce explicit abstractions for settings access, secret resolution, cache paths, trace sinks, and clock/network probes so the engine is not tied directly to user-profile helpers or UI-era service classes. A future PortfolioSaver.DataService host may run the same DataEngine later, but the refactor should not depend on introducing a Windows service immediately.

Non-goal: do not attempt a big-bang rewrite, do not re-architect the locked VM harness in the process, and do not start by adding arbitrary multithreading. Parallel provider execution should be a controlled outcome of the new engine boundary, not the first step.

Phase 0 - dependency audit and boundary contracts: before moving logic, catalog every concrete dependency currently new'ed inside StartupCoordinator and related runtime services, then introduce abstractions for settings access, secret resolution, cache/storage access, trace logging, network availability, time, and provider factories. Acceptance: DataEngine can be composed from contracts rather than constructing environment-bound helpers internally.

Phase 1 - seam definition: define engine-facing contracts for quote snapshots, quote-refresh requests/results, provider execution plans, freshness anchors, startup readiness, and historical/news work items. During this phase, copy as little behavior as possible; prefer extracting interfaces and pure helper types first. Acceptance: Presentation can depend on an engine contract instead of directly owning provider ladder decisions.

Phase 2 - extract scheduler and provider orchestration: move refresh-window building, due-symbol selection, stagger logic, provider plan ordering, rate-limit cooldown handling, partial-result handling, and quote-merge logic out of StartupCoordinator into DataEngine services. Keep concurrency behavior semantically equivalent at first. Acceptance: unit tests can validate scheduling and provider fallback behavior without constructing WPF controls or scene state.

Phase 3 - extract startup/warmup and freshness policies: move initial stale-data recovery logic, dedicated Yahoo warmup rules, graph warmup coordination, startup readiness thresholds, and status freshness anchor calculation into the engine layer. Acceptance: the engine can produce a clean startup state model such as loading, warming, live, partial, stale without the scene control owning the logic directly.

Phase 4 - extract news orchestration and runtime settings access: move summarized news scheduling, feed selection cadence, cache decisions, and teleprinter item preparation into engine-facing services while keeping the visual teleprinter playback itself in Presentation. At the same time, split settings read/write concerns from runtime settings consumption so the engine depends on a read model rather than the settings UI service classes directly. Acceptance: news retrieval and news rendering become distinct responsibilities and the engine is no longer coupled to VisualizerSettingsService.

Phase 5 - scene adaptation and namespace cleanup: reduce StartupCoordinator to a thin adapter that asks DataEngine for a state snapshot and maps that into VisualizerSceneState and view models. Rename or relocate residual runtime classes out of PortfolioSaver.Presentation.Services where appropriate so the desktop-first architecture is reflected clearly. Acceptance: StartupCoordinator becomes a compositional facade instead of the core runtime brain, and service names/namespaces no longer imply legacy ownership of the modern runtime layer.

Phase 6 - optional controlled concurrency: once the engine owns scheduling, add bounded async worker lanes by concern or provider group, for example Yahoo quotes, provider fallbacks, historical warmup, news, and treasury/macros. Use bounded concurrency, explicit cooldown/budget gates, deterministic merge rules, and structured tracing. Acceptance: parallelism improves cadence without introducing nondeterministic UI regressions.

Phase 7 - future service host feasibility review: only after the in-process DataEngine is stable should we evaluate adding a PortfolioSaver.DataService Windows service host. That later review must explicitly address secrets ownership, per-user versus machine-wide settings, IPC contract choice such as named pipes or gRPC over named pipes, installer behavior, and support burden. This ticket does not require implementing the service host itself.

Key risks to manage: duplicated logic during migration, freshness regressions, cache/secrets path confusion, over-eager concurrency creating race conditions, over-coupling the engine to user-profile storage, and accidental coupling back from Presentation into the engine. Mitigations: move one concern at a time, keep trace semantics stable, add regression tests before each extraction, and insist on small commits that preserve the canonical VM proof path.

Required regression coverage during the refactor: scheduling tests, provider fallback tests, stale/fresh classification tests, startup readiness tests, news cadence tests, graph warmup tests, settings/secrets abstraction tests, and at each major phase a canonical VM proof through the locked harness. No phase should be considered complete if local tests are green but the canonical VM path is broken.

Definition of done for the full ticket: a new engine layer exists; StartupCoordinator is dramatically reduced and no longer owns most provider orchestration logic; Presentation consumes engine snapshots rather than managing retrieval policy directly; provider scheduling is testable without WPF; settings and secret access are abstracted cleanly enough that a later service host would not require another deep untangling; the canonical VM harness remains the validation baseline; and the resulting architecture is ready for a later optional Windows service host without forcing another major refactor.
Deferred from the current beta lane to the next major release so the refactor can be planned and executed as a deliberate architecture program rather than mixed into current stabilization work.
Not a beta-blocker for the current lane as long as the existing locked harness and data/UI behavior remain stable enough for ongoing product fixes.

change_requests.title: Replace the in-process YFinance runtime with a standalone YFinance.NET client-server architecture
evidence: User requested replacing the old service-ready DataEngine concept with a pure client-server architecture where YFinance.NET runs as its own process and the UI becomes a sequential client.
notes: This ticket completely replaces NB-023 as the active architecture program.
Separate YFinance.NET fully into its own process with its own circular log file and runtime lifecycle.
The YFinance.NET server must listen on TCP port 14870 and accept client connections from any IP address.
The server must support multiple client connections with a maximum of 1024 concurrent clients.
Design the server so it can run on a completely separate machine from the UI client in the future.

Long-range portability target: keep the architecture and protocol clean enough that the YFinance.NET server can later be reimplemented or migrated to cross-platform standard C++ for Linux/Unix/Windows/Windows-XP/macOS Intel/macOS ARM/Raspberry Pi and related platforms.
Define a network protocol between the UI and the YFinance.NET server, ideally echoing the clarity of Yahoo v7-style request/response semantics, while remaining our own stable product protocol.

Document the protocol in a dedicated Interface Control Document (ICD) kept in the project repository, and treat that ICD as a maintained project artifact that evolves with implementation changes and test expectations.

The client-server protocol must be minimal but sufficient: no speculative complexity, but enough structure to cleanly support the required request types, cache semantics, server metadata, and explicit error states.

Protocol responses must include explicit exception scenarios the UI can handle cleanly, such as Network Lost, Upstream Server Not Responding, upstream throttled, invalid symbol, and cache miss or stale-result states where relevant.

Async server messages are limited to server or connection lifecycle events, not ordinary market-data flow. Normal quote/history/timing failures should be returned as request-scoped error responses, not unsolicited pushes.
Primary protocol model: client-driven request/response. The UI client owns request initiation and pacing; the server answers requests and does not become the UI scheduler.

Ordinary lookup and upstream failures must remain request-scoped error responses. Async server exception messages are reserved for server-wide or connection-wide conditions such as shutdown, overload, idle timeout, or protocol violation.

Preserve upstream-sync friendliness: the clean-room YFinance.NET port must remain easy to keep in sync with future changes from the user's upstream Python fork, and the new client-server split must not destroy that maintainability goal.

YFinance.NET server behavior for single or batch ticker requests: first check cache, return cached values when they are newer than the 10-minute freshness ceiling, otherwise fetch from Yahoo, return the fresh data, and store it back in cache.
Nothing served from cache should be older than 10 minutes unless the protocol intentionally marks it as stale under a future degraded-mode extension.

Any client identifier sent upstream to Yahoo must be a unique random hash derived from the requesting machine identity and must not include the author name, organization name, or other human-identifying product branding.

Once the caching YFinance.NET server is functional, the UI should no longer carry throttling responsibility. The UI should request macros one by one during warmup, then global exchanges one by one, then continue sequential retrieval from YFinance.NET with approximately 500 milliseconds (0.5 seconds) spacing after each UI update so visual update flares remain continuous while CPU load stays controlled.

No parallel connections from the same UI client to YFinance.NET. Multi-client server support exists so one shared server can eventually support many desktop UIs across a network, not so a single UI floods the server with parallel requests.

Server lifecycle must support two modes: owned mode and standalone mode. The default product mode for now is owned mode, where the UI launches the YFinance.NET server and the server exits when the owning UI process or session goes away.

UI configuration changes should normally affect only client-side request sequencing and symbol selection. They should not generally mutate server internals; the server should expose only a small admin/control surface such as health, status, optional shutdown, and optional cache flush operations.

This is a major refactor and includes test script updates, harness updates, starting and stopping YFinance.NET alongside the UI for now, documentation updates, and forensic code-review cleanup revealed during the transition.

Acceptance should include a clean end-to-end UI proof with the standalone YFinance.NET server process, updated harness lifecycle management, updated docs, and removal of obsolete in-process retrieval assumptions from the active code path.

All request, response, and async event messages now carry a local-time timestamp with UTC offset plus an uppercase SHA-256 payload checksum.

All client/server communications are now logged into the dedicated UI and YFinance circular trace files, including request send/receive, response send/receive, integrity verification, and lifecycle events.

change_requests.title: Analyze Microsoft Store migration from Inno installer to MSIX packaging
evidence: User requested analysis of Microsoft Store requirements, the implications of moving from Inno Setup to MSIX, and whether Store approval avoids paid code-signing certificate costs.
User explicitly selected the target path: Microsoft Store + MSIX, with $0 developer registration, $0 certification fee, and $0 Microsoft-managed MSIX signing as the desired distribution strategy.
research: Microsoft Learn Code signing options for Windows app developers states that if an app is published as an MSIX package through the Microsoft Store, code signing is free and handled automatically because Microsoft re-signs the package after certification; no certificate purchase/management is required for Store MSIX distribution: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/package-and-deploy/code-signing-options.

The same Microsoft code-signing guidance states that if publishing an MSI/EXE installer through the Store, the developer remains responsible for Authenticode signing the installer before submission: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/package-and-deploy/code-signing-options.

Microsoft Learn Sign an MSIX package explains development/test signing options including WinApp CLI, SignTool, unsigned testing packages, Azure Artifact Signing, and Device Guard signing: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/msix/package/signing-package-overview.

Microsoft Learn guidance for distributing Win32 applications through the Microsoft Store covers MSIX-based Store distribution and recommends Windows App Certification Kit validation for Store compliance: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/distribute-through-store/how-to-distribute-your-win32-app-through-microsoft-store.

Microsoft Store get-started documentation states MSIX/PWA submissions enter certification, where Microsoft performs security tests, technical compliance tests, and content compliance checks, with certification taking up to three business days: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/publish/get-started.
acceptance: Lock the intended distribution target to Microsoft Store + MSIX, not MSI/EXE/Inno submission through the Store.
Treat avoidance of recurring paid Authenticode certificate costs as a core requirement of this CR.
Produce a project-native MSIX migration design document comparing current Inno Setup release flow with a Store/MSIX release flow.

Confirm and document that the current Microsoft Store + MSIX path has $0 developer registration, $0 certification fee, and $0 Microsoft-managed MSIX signing cost under current Microsoft onboarding/signing guidance.
Document the important boundary condition that MSI/EXE/Inno Store submissions do not satisfy this requirement because developer-managed Authenticode signing remains required for those artifacts.

Inventory required package identity, publisher identity, app manifest, assets/icons, capabilities, file associations/protocols if any, install/uninstall behavior, Local AppData behavior, startup/background process behavior, and YFinance.NET server bundling implications.

Analyze whether the app can be packaged as MSIX without breaking owned YFinance.NET server launch, configuration app launch, shortcut behavior, user data location, background image asset/download behavior, and future update/uninstall cleanup expectations.

Identify required build pipeline changes, likely tooling options, developer/test signing approach, Windows App Certification Kit validation, Store Partner Center steps, and release documentation changes.
Recommend whether to replace Inno entirely, support both Inno and MSIX in parallel during transition, or defer Store/MSIX until specific blockers are resolved.
If implementation is approved after analysis, create follow-on implementation CRs for MSIX package generation, Store certification validation, and release pipeline integration.
notes: Project decision: the desired path is Microsoft Store + MSIX specifically because it is the currently documented $0 path for onboarding/certification/MSIX signing.
Initial research indicates the Store/MSIX path can solve the paid certificate problem for Store distribution because Microsoft re-signs certified MSIX packages.
Initial research also indicates keeping EXE/MSI/Inno as the Store submission artifact would not solve signing, because Authenticode signing remains our responsibility for MSI/EXE Store submissions.
The Inno/GitHub release path may remain useful as a fallback or parallel channel, but it is no longer the preferred primary public trust path if MSIX/Store proves technically feasible.
This CR is analysis-first because MSIX may affect app identity, process model, installed paths, update behavior, and multi-executable packaging.
